headline: The West Bar Rebuilt Itself Again — Fish the New Seam, Not Last Month's Spot
subhead: Moriches Inlet's bottom shifted under the July swell, and the bass and blues found the new edge before most anglers did.
body_markdown:
I ran the skiff through the cut Tuesday morning on a dropping tide and the depth finder told me something the charts won't show you for another year: the west bar off Cupsogue has built back in, maybe two feet shallower than it was in June, and the main channel has squeezed itself against the Westhampton side. That's not unusual for August — the inlet does this every summer as the longshore drift piles sand off the jetty stub and the current finds the path of least resistance — but it matters this week because the fish have already relocated to the new seam, and a lot of guys are still working water that isn't holding structure anymore.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the real story here wouldn't be this weekend, it'd be what shows up once the tidal range builds into the August 12 new moon. That's exactly what's happening. The moon is pulling harder water through the cut every day now, and that increased flow is doing what it always does at Moriches: sharpening the edges, concentrating bait, and giving the bass a reason to stack instead of scatter.

Right now the best window is the last two hours of the outgoing on the ocean side of the inlet, right where that new west bar drops into the channel. I'm marking bait — peanut bunker and rainfish — getting pinned against that edge as the water pulls out, and the bass are using the deeper cut like a funnel. Bucktails in the 1.5-ounce range, white or olive, cast up-current and allowed to swing down along the drop, are outproducing everything else I've tried. Let it hit bottom once, then keep it just ticking the sand on a slow retrieve — the takes are coming right where the seam meets the flat, not out in the open water. Sizes have been mixed, mostly high-twenties to low-30-inch fish, with the occasional slot pushing 34. Nothing epic, but honest fish on a consistent pattern, and that's worth more to me than a one-day blitz.

Cupsogue itself has been decent from the beach for the same reason — that outgoing water dumping bait past the swimming beach and around the point gives surfcasters a real shot if they're willing to walk. I talked to a guy Thursday who worked the stretch between the second and third parking field with a Danny swimmer at first light and had three fish to 30 inches before the sun got high. That's the kind of report I trust — not a blitz, just a guy who understood the tide stage and put himself in front of moving water.

Bluefish have been the wildcard. Some mornings the birds are working bunker schools right off the inlet mouth and you'll see gators in the 8-to-12-pound class ripping through, other mornings it's dead calm and you'd swear there isn't a blue in the bay. My read is they're following the same bunker pods pushing tight to the beach that we're seeing region-wide right now, and they're not committing to Moriches specifically — they're just passing through when the bait funnels past. If you see working birds off Tuthill Point or the inlet mouth, don't wait, get on it, because that window closes fast.

Fluke fishing inside the bay has been steady but unspectacular — the kind of bite where you need to move to find quality. The channel edges off Pattersquash and the deeper holes toward Tuthill Point have given up keepers to 4 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and bucktails, drifted slow on the last of the outgoing when the water's still got some push to it. Slack tide has been dead there — no current, no drift, no bites, which tells you the fluke in this bay are still ambush feeders working current lines rather than roaming the flats in this warm water.

Weakfish have been scattered and honestly disappointing — a few reports of fish in the 2-to-3-pound range around the deeper holes near the Moriches Inlet bridge on soft plastics fished slow along bottom, but nothing you could call a pattern yet. Porgies are more reliable if you want steady action — anchoring up on the deeper structure inside the bay near the Inlet with sandworms or clam has been producing good numbers of scup in the 10-to-12-inch range, a solid bend-your-rod option on a day when the current-driven bite isn't cooperating.

Looking ahead, the building tidal range through the August 12 new moon should keep sharpening that cut bite at the inlet — more water moving means more bait getting pinned, more bass committing to the seam instead of holding loose. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't blow the inlet dirty, I'd fish that new west bar drop on the last two hours of the outgoing through the weekend and into early next week. If a blow does come through and reshapes that bar again, don't assume the spot — go find where the new cut is before you start casting. This inlet rewards anglers who read the bottom, not the memory of where the fish were last month.
